claim: Visual categorization in adults is amazingly rapid, occurring in about one-tenth of a second.
source: Visual categorization is important for everyday activities and is amazingly rapid: adults categorize the visual input in about one-tenth of a second (Thorpe et al., 1996; Grill-Spector and Kanwisher, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Thorpe et al., 1996 and Grill-Spector and Kanwisher, 2005

claim: Visual categorization in adults and school-age children is supported by both clustered and distributed responses to visual categories in ventral temporal and lateral occipitotemporal cortex.
source: In adults and school-age children, this key behavior is supported by both clustered and distributed responses to visual categories in high-level visual cortex in ventral temporal and lateral occipitotemporal cortex (VTC and LOTC, respectively) (Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014; Bugatus et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014 and Bugatus et al., 2017

claim: A visual category consists of items that share common visual features and configurations.
source: A visual category consists of items that share common visual features and configurations (Grill-Spector and Kanwisher, 2005; Nordt et al., 2021; Margalit et al., 2020; Gomez et al., 2017; Stigliani et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work defining visual categories

claim: Corridors share features of floors, walls, and ceilings with a typical spatial relationship.
source: e.g., corridors share features of floors, walls, and ceilings, with a typical spatial relationship.
evidence: Provided as an example of common visual features and configurations in a category

claim: Clustered regions in VTC and LOTC respond more strongly to items of ecologically relevant categories (faces, bodies, places, words) than other stimuli.
source: Clustered regions in VTC and LOTC (Bugatus et al., 2017; Haxby et al., 2001; Nordt et al., 2023) respond more strongly to items of ecologically relevant categories (faces, bodies, places, words) than other stimuli (Nordt et al., 2021; Kanwisher et al., 1997; Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998; Downing et al., 2001; Golarai et al., 2007; Scherf et al., 2007; Dehaene-Lambertz et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior neuroimaging studies

claim: Distributed neural responses across VTC and LOTC are reliable across items of a category but distinct across items of different categories.
source: and distributed neural responses across VTC and LOTC (Bugatus et al., 2017; Haxby et al., 2001; Nordt et al., 2023) are reliable across items of a category but distinct across items of different categories.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior neuroimaging studies

claim: It is unknown when visual category representations emerge in infants' brains.
source: However, it is unknown when these visual category representations emerge in infants' brains.
evidence: Statement of the research gap motivating the study

claim: Between 4 and 10 months of age, infants can behaviorally distinguish between faces and objects.
source: between 4 and 10 months of age, infants can behaviorally distinguish between faces and objects (Spriet et al., 2022; Mondloch et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral studies

claim: Between 4 and 10 months of age, infants can behaviorally distinguish between different animals like cats and dogs.
source: between 4 and 10 months of age, infants can behaviorally distinguish between faces and objects (Spriet et al., 2022; Mondloch et al., 1999) and between different animals like cats and dogs (Quinn et al., 1993; Younger and Fearing, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral studies

claim: Between 10 and 19 months, infants behaviorally distinguish broader-level animate vs. inanimate categories.
source: Later on, between 10 and 19 months, infants behaviorally distinguish broader-level animate vs. inanimate categories (Spriet et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to behavioral study

claim: EEG studies have found stronger responses to images of faces vs. objects or textures in 4- to 12-month-olds.
source: Neurally, electroencephalographic (EEG) studies have found stronger responses to images of faces vs. objects or textures in 4- to 12-month-olds (Conte et al., 2020; Farzin et al., 2012; de Heering and Rossion, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior EEG studies

claim: Stimulus category can be decoded from distributed responses slightly but significantly above chance in 6- to 15-month-olds.
source: and that stimulus category can be decoded from distributed responses slightly but significantly above chance in 6- to 15-month-olds (Bayet et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior EEG studies

claim: fMRI studies have found stronger responses to videos of faces vs. objects in clustered regions in VTC and LOTC of 2- to 10-month-olds.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies have found stronger responses to videos of faces (Deen et al., 2017; Kosakowski et al., 2022), bodies (Kosakowski et al., 2022), and places (Deen et al., 2017; Kosakowski et al., 2022) vs. objects in clustered regions in VTC and LOTC of 2- to 10-month-olds.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior fMRI studies

claim: fMRI studies have found stronger responses to videos of bodies vs. objects in clustered regions in VTC and LOTC of 2- to 10-month-olds.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies have found stronger responses to videos of faces (Deen et al., 2017; Kosakowski et al., 2022), bodies (Kosakowski et al., 2022), and places (Deen et al., 2017; Kosakowski et al., 2022) vs. objects in clustered regions in VTC and LOTC of 2- to 10-month-olds.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior fMRI studies

claim: fMRI studies have found stronger responses to videos of places vs. objects in clustered regions in VTC and LOTC of 2- to 10-month-olds.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies have found stronger responses to videos of faces (Deen et al., 2017; Kosakowski et al., 2022), bodies (Kosakowski et al., 2022), and places (Deen et al., 2017; Kosakowski et al., 2022) vs. objects in clustered regions in VTC and LOTC of 2- to 10-month-olds.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior fMRI studies

claim: Prior studies used different types of stimuli and age ranges, making it unknown when representations to various categories emerge during the first year of life.
source: However, because prior studies used different types of stimuli and age ranges, it is unknown when representations to various categories emerge during the first year of life.
evidence: Statement of research gap based on limitations of prior work

claim: Selective responses to faces, places, and body parts have been found in VTC and LOTC of 2- to 10-month-olds.
source: Supporting this hypothesis are findings of (i) selective responses to faces, places, and body parts in VTC and LOTC of 2- to 10-month-olds (Kosakowski et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior fMRI study

claim: Above chance classification of distributed EEG responses to toys, bodies, faces, houses has been found in 6- to 8-month-olds.
source: and (ii) above chance classification of distributed EEG responses to toys, bodies, faces, houses in 6- to 8-month-olds (Xie et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior EEG study

claim: Above chance classification of distributed EEG responses to animals and body parts has been found in 12- to 15-month-olds.
source: as well as animals and body parts in 12- to 15-month-olds (Bayet et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior EEG study

claim: Representations of ecologically relevant categories like faces, body parts, and places may be innate because of their evolutionary importance.
source: First, representations of ecologically relevant categories like faces, body parts, and places may be innate because of their evolutionary importance (Kanwisher, 2010; Sugita, 2009; Mahon and Caramazza, 2011; Bi et al., 2016)
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citations to theoretical papers

claim: Representations for categories other than faces, body parts, and places may develop later only with learning.
source: whereas representations for other categories may develop later only with learning (Nordt et al., 2021; Nordt et al., 2023; Behrmann and Plaut, 2015).
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Newborns and young infants tend to orient to faces.
source: Supporting this hypothesis are findings that newborns and young infants tend to orient to faces (Pascalis et al., 1995)
evidence: Supported by citation to behavioral study

claim: Newborns and young infants tend to orient to face-like stimuli.
source: and face-like stimuli (Johnson et al., 1991)
evidence: Supported by citation to behavioral study

claim: Newborns and young infants have cortical responses to face-like stimuli.
source: as well as have cortical responses to face-like stimuli (Buiatti et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to neuroimaging study

claim: Word representations only emerge in childhood with the onset of reading instruction.
source: but word representations only emerge in childhood with the onset of reading instruction (Nordt et al., 2021; Nordt et al., 2023; Dehaene et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Visual experience is necessary for the development of category representations, including faces.
source: Second, even if visual experience is necessary for the development category representations (including faces; Arcaro et al., 2019; Scott and Arcaro, 2023; Livingstone et al., 2017; Arcaro et al., 2017)
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Categories that are seen more frequently earlier in infancy may develop before others.
source: categories that are seen more frequently earlier in infancy may develop before others.
evidence: Hypothesis based on visual experience

claim: The visual diet of 0- to 3-month-olds contains approximately 25% faces and less than 10% hands.
source: The visual diet of 0- to 3-month-olds contains ~25% faces and <10% hands, that of 12- to 15-month-olds contains ~20% faces and ~20% hands (Fausey et al., 2016; Jayaraman et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to studies using head-mounted cameras

claim: The visual diet of 12- to 15-month-olds contains approximately 20% faces and approximately 20% hands.
source: The visual diet of 0- to 3-month-olds contains ~25% faces and <10% hands, that of 12- to 15-month-olds contains ~20% faces and ~20% hands (Fausey et al., 2016; Jayaraman et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to studies using head-mounted cameras

claim: The visual diet of 24-month-olds contains approximately 10% faces and approximately 25% hands.
source: and that of 24-month-olds contains ~10% faces, and ~25% hands.
evidence: Inferred from prior sentence citing Fausey et al., 2016 and Jayaraman et al., 2017

claim: Looking behavior in infants predicts that representations of faces may emerge before that of limbs.
source: Thus, looking behavior in infants predicts that representations of faces may emerge before that of limbs.
evidence: Prediction based on visual diet data from prior studies

claim: 45 infants from four age groups participated in the study: 3–4 months (n=17, 7 females), 4–6 months (n=14, 7 females), 6–8 months (n=15, 6 females), and 12–15 months (n=15, 4 females).
source: 45 infants from four age groups: 3–4 months (n=17, 7 females), 4–6 months (n=14, 7 females), 6–8 months (n=15, 6 females), and 12–15 months (n=15, 4 females) participated in EEG experiments.
evidence: Description of study participants

claim: Twelve participants were part of an ongoing longitudinal study and came for several sessions spanning at least 3 months apart.
source: Twelve participants were part of an ongoing longitudinal study and came for several sessions spanning at least 3 months apart.
evidence: Description of study design

claim: Infants viewed gray-scale images from five visual categories: faces, limbs, corridors, characters, and cars.
source: Infants viewed gray-scale images from five visual categories present in infants' environments (faces, limbs, corridors, characters, and cars) while EEG was recorded.
evidence: Description of experimental stimuli

claim: The images used in this study have been widely used in fMRI studies and are largely controlled for low-level properties such as luminance, contrast, similarity, and spatial frequency.
source: Different from prior infant studies (Conte et al., 2020; de Heering and Rossion, 2015; Bayet et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2022; Deen et al., 2017; Kosakowski et al., 2022), we used images that have been widely used in fMRI studies (Nordt et al., 2021; Gomez et al., 2017; Allen et al., 2022; Lerma-Usabiaga et al., 2018; Jagadeesh and Gardner, 2022) and are largely controlled for low-level properties such as luminance, contrast, similarity, and spatial frequency (Figure 1B and Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1B showing stimulus properties

claim: In the SSVEP paradigm, images from five categories were shown every 0.233 s, with one category as the target appearing every 1.167 s.
source: We use a steady-state visual evoked potential (de Heering and Rossion, 2015; Farzin et al., 2012; Heinrich et al., 2009; Liu-Shuang et al., 2014) (SSVEP) paradigm: In each 70 s sequence, images from five categories were shown every 0.233 s; one of the categories was the target, so different images from that category appeared every 1.167 s, and the rest of the images were drawn from the other four categories in a random order (Figure 1A).
evidence: Description of experimental paradigm with reference to Figure 1A

claim: Images of all categories appeared at equal probability and no images were repeated within a sequence.
source: Images of all categories appeared at equal probability and no images were repeated (Stigliani et al., 2015).
evidence: Description of stimulus presentation with citation

claim: The EEG-SSVEP approach affords a high signal-to-noise ratio with short acquisitions making it effective for infants.
source: We used the EEG-SSVEP approach because: (i) it affords a high signal-to-noise ratio with short acquisitions making it effective for infants (de Heering and Rossion, 2015; Farzin et al., 2012)
evidence: Rationale for method choice supported by citations

claim: The EEG-SSVEP approach has been successfully used to study responses to faces in infants.
source: (ii) it has been successfully used to study responses to faces in infants (de Heering and Rossion, 2015; Farzin et al., 2012; Rekow et al., 2021)
evidence: Rationale for method choice supported by citations

claim: The EEG-SSVEP approach enables measuring both general visual response to images at 4.286 Hz and category-selective responses at 0.857 Hz.
source: and (iii) it enables measuring both general visual response to images by examining responses at the image presentation frequency (4.286 Hz) and category-selective responses by examining responses at the category frequency (0.857 Hz, Figure 1A).
evidence: Description of method capabilities with reference to Figure 1A

claim: Category-selective responses can be reliably measured using EEG-SSVEP in adults with the same amount of data as in infants.
source: Results in adults validate the SSVEP paradigm for measuring category selectivity: as they show that (i) category-selective responses can be reliably measured using EEG-SSVEP with the same amount of data as in infants (Appendix 1—figure 1, Appendix 1—figure 2)
evidence: Validation results with reference to supplementary figures

claim: Category information from distributed spatiotemporal response patterns can be decoded in adults with the same amount of data as in infants.
source: and that (ii) category information from distributed spatiotemporal response patterns can be decoded with the same amount of data as in infants (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: Validation results with reference to supplementary figure

claim: Despite being blurry when filtered to match 3-month-old cortical acuity, images of different categories are readily distinguishable by adults.
source: Despite being blurry, images of different categories are readily distinguishable by adults (Videos 1–5), suggesting that there is sufficient visual information in the lower spatial frequencies of the stimuli for infants to distinguish visual categories.
evidence: Observation from stimulus validation with reference to videos

claim: In all infant age groups, visual responses were concentrated spatially over occipital electrodes.
source: We found that in all age groups, visual responses were concentrated spatially over occipital electrodes (Figure 2A–D, left panel, Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: Experimental finding with reference to Figure 2

claim: Significant visual responses were found in all infant age groups at the image frequency and its first three harmonics over the occipital ROI.
source: Quantification of the mean visual response amplitude over a region of interest (ROI) spanning nine electrodes over early visual cortex (occipital ROI) revealed significant responses in all infant age groups at the image frequency and its first three harmonics (response amplitudes significantly above zero with false discovery rate [FDR] corrected at four levels; except for the first harmonic at 8.571 Hz in 6- to 8-month-olds; Figure 2A–D, right panel).
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data with reference to Figure 2

claim: Visual responses were not significantly different across category conditions.
source: Analysis of visual responses separately by category condition revealed that visual responses were not significantly different across category conditions (Appendix 1—figure 5; no significant main effect of category, βcategory = 0.08, 95% CI: –0.08–0.24, t(301) = 0.97, p=0.33, or category by age interaction, βcategory × age = -0.04, 95% CI: –0.11–0.03, t(301) = –1.09, p=0.28, linear mixed model (LMM) on response amplitude to 4.286 Hz and its first three harmonics).
evidence: Statistical analysis with LMM and reference to supplementary figure

claim: There was no significant difference in noise across age groups.
source: We found no significant difference in noise across age groups (Figure 2E).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to Figure 2E

claim: Temporal waveforms had two deflections in 3- to 4-month-olds (one negativity and one positivity).
source: We observed that during the 233 ms image presentation, temporal waveforms had two deflections in 3- to 4-month-olds (one negativity and one positivity, Figure 2F)
evidence: Observation from time-domain analysis with reference to Figure 2F

claim: Temporal waveforms had four deflections for infants older than 4 months (two minima and two maxima).
source: and four deflections for infants older than 4 months (two minima and two maxima, Figure 2F).
evidence: Observation from time-domain analysis with reference to Figure 2F

claim: The latency of the peak visual response deflection decreased from 3 to 15 months.
source: In general, we find that the latency of the peak deflection decreased from 3 to 15 months (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to Figures 2G and H

claim: The latency of the peak deflection significantly and differentially decreased with age in the two time windows.
source: Results reveal that the latency of the peak deflection significantly and differentially decreased with age in the two time windows (βage × time window = –45.78, 95% CI: –58.39 to –33.17, t(118) = –7.19, p=6.39 × 10–11; LMM with age and time window as fixed effects, and participant as a random effect, all stats in Appendix 1—table 4, Appendix 1—table 5).
evidence: Statistical analysis using LMM with reference to supplementary tables

claim: There were larger decreases in the peak latency in the second than first time window.
source: There were larger decreases in the peak latency in the second than first time window (Figure 2G and H, first:βage = –7.44, 95% CI: –13.82 to –1.06, t(118) = –2.33, pFDR<0.05; second: βage = –46.91, 95% CI: –56.56 to –37.27, t(59) = –9.73, pFDR<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to Figures 2G and H

claim: Peak amplitude differentially develops across the two time windows.
source: Peak amplitude also differentially develops across the two windows (βage × time window = –4.90, 95% CI: –8.66 to –1.14, t(118) = –2.58, p=0.01, Appendix 1—table 6, Appendix 1—table 7).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to supplementary tables

claim: The decrease in peak amplitude with age was significant only for the second deflection.
source: The decrease in peak amplitude with age was significant only for the second deflection (βage = –3.59, 95% CI: –6.38 to –0.81, t(59) = –2.58, p=0.01, LMM).
evidence: Statistical analysis using LMM

claim: The temporal dynamics of visual responses over occipital cortex develop from 3 to 15 months of age.
source: These data suggest that the temporal dynamics of visual responses over occipital cortex develop from 3 to 15 months of age.
evidence: Interpretation of statistical analyses of latency and amplitude data

claim: Significant categorical responses to faces were observed over bilateral occipitotemporal electrodes in 4- to 6-month-olds at 0.857 Hz.
source: Notably, there were significant responses to faces over bilateral occipitotemporal electrodes in 4- to 6-month-olds at 0.857 Hz (Figure 3B, response amplitudes significantly above zero with Hotelling's T2 statistic, pFDR<0.05, FDR corrected over two levels: the category frequency and its first harmonic)
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to Figure 3B

claim: Significant categorical responses to faces were observed in 6- to 8-month-olds and 12- to 15-month-olds at the category frequency and its first harmonic.
source: as well as 6- to 8-month-olds and 12- to 15-month-olds at the category frequency and its first harmonic (Figure 3C and D, both pFDR<0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to Figures 3C and D

claim: There were no significant responses to faces in 3- to 4-month-olds at either the category frequency or its harmonics.
source: However, there were no significant responses to faces in 3- to 4-month-olds at either the category frequency or its harmonics (Figure 3A, right panel).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to Figure 3A

claim: Face-selective responses start to reliably emerge over lateral occipitotemporal cortex between 4 and 6 months of age.
source: These data suggest that face-selective responses start to reliably emerge over lateral occipitotemporal cortex between 4 and 6 months of age.
evidence: Interpretation of statistical analyses of face-selective responses

claim: Significant category-selective responses were found for limbs in 6- to 8-month-olds in the ROT ROI.
source: Instead, we found significant category-selective responses that survived FDR correction for (i) limbs in 6- to 8-month-olds in the ROT ROI (Appendix 1—figure 6)
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to supplementary figure

claim: Significant category-selective responses were found for corridors in 6- to 8-month-olds and 12- to 15-months-old in the LOT ROI.
source: (ii) corridors in 6- to 8-month-olds and 12- to 15-months-old in the left occipitotemporal (LOT) ROI (Appendix 1—figure 7)
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to supplementary figure

claim: Significant category-selective responses were found for characters in 6- to 8-month-olds in the ROT ROI, and in 12- to 15-month-olds in bilateral occipitotemporal ROI.
source: and (iii) characters in 6- to 8-month-olds in the ROT ROI, and in 12- to 15-month-olds in bilateral occipitotemporal ROI (Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to supplementary figure

claim: There was significant development of response amplitudes in both occipitotemporal ROIs which varied by category.
source: With an LMM analysis, we found significant development of response amplitudes in both the occipitotemporal ROIs which varied by category (LOT ROIs: βcategory × age = –0.21, 95% CI: –0.39 to –0.04, t(301) = –2.40, pFDR<0.05; ROT ROIs: βcategory × age = –0.26, 95% CI: –0.48 to –0.03, t(301) = –2.26, pFDR<0.05, LMM as a function of log (age) and category; participant: random effect).
evidence: Statistical analysis using LMM

claim: Average temporal waveforms over lateral-occipital ROIs show significant responses to faces that emerge at approximately 4 months of age.
source: Consistent with frequency domain analyses, average temporal waveforms over lateral-occipital ROIs show significant responses to faces that emerge at ~4 months of age (Figure 4A, significant responses relative to zero, cluster-based nonparametric permutation 10,000 times, two-tailed t-test, at p<0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to Figure 4A

claim: The temporal waveforms of responses to faces in infants show an initial positive deflection peaking at approximately 500 ms after stimulus onset followed by a negative deflection peaking at approximately 900 ms.
source: The temporal waveforms of responses to faces in infants show an initial positive deflection peaking ~500 ms after stimulus onset followed by a negative deflection peaking at ~900 ms.
evidence: Observation from time-domain analysis

claim: Mean waveforms associated with limbs, corridors, and characters in lateral occipital ROIs show only a single negative deflection that peaks at approximately 500 ms after stimulus onset.
source: Notably, mean waveforms associated with limbs, corridors, and characters in lateral occipital ROIs are different from faces: there is only a single negative deflection that peaks at ~500 ms after stimulus onset, which is significant only in 6- to 8- and 12- to 15-month-olds (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Observation from time-domain analysis with reference to Figures 4B-D

claim: There was no significant category response to cars in infants except for a late (approximately 1000 ms) positive response in 4- to 6-month-olds.
source: There was no significant category response to cars in infants except for a late (~1000 ms) positive response in 4- to 6-month-olds (Figure 4E).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to Figure 4E

claim: The timing and waveform differ across categories, suggesting additional category information in the distributed spatiotemporal response.
source: These results show that both the timing and waveform differ across categories, which suggests that there might be additional category information in the distributed spatiotemporal response.
evidence: Inference from observations of waveform differences

claim: There was significant development of the peak response in the right lateral occipitotemporal ROI which varied by category.
source: We found significant development of the peak response in the right lateral occipitotemporal ROI which varied by category (βcategory × age = –1.09, 95% CI: –2.00 to –0.14, t(301) = –2.26, pFDR<0.05, LMM as a function of log(age) and category; participant: random effect).
evidence: Statistical analysis using LMM

claim: The peak response for faces significantly increased from 3 to 15 months.
source: Post hoc analyses revealed that the peak response for faces significantly increased from 3 to 15 months (Figure 4A right, βage = 7.27, 95% CI: 4.03–10.51, t(59) = 4.50, pFDR<0.05, LMM as a function of log(age); participant: random effect)
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to Figure 4A

claim: The peak response for limbs significantly decreased from 3 to 15 months.
source: and the peak response for limbs significantly decreased (Figure 4B right, βage = –2.90, 95% CI: –5.41 to –0.38, t(59) = –2.31, p=0.02, not significant after FDR correction over five category levels).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to Figure 4B

claim: For all categories, the latency of the peak response in the ROT ROI significantly decreased from 3 to 15 months of age.
source: Additionally, for all categories, the latency of the peak response in the ROT ROI significantly decreased from 3 to 15 months of age (βage = –173.17, 95% CI: –284.73 to –61.61, t(301) = –3.05, p=0.002, LMM as a function of log(age) and category; participant: random effect).
evidence: Statistical analysis using LMM

claim: There was no significant development of peak latency in the LOT ROI.
source: We found no significant development of peak latency in the LOT ROI (Appendix 1—table 8, Appendix 1—table 9).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to supplementary tables

claim: The LOOCV classifier decoded category information from brain responses significantly above the 20% chance level in infants aged 6 months and older but not in younger infants.
source: Results reveal two main findings. First, the LOOCV classifier decoded category information from brain responses significantly above the 20% chance level in infants aged 6 months and older but not in younger infants (Figure 5B, 6- to 8-month-olds, significant above chance: t(14) = 4.1, pFDR<0.01, one-tailed, FDR corrected over four age groups; 12- to 15-month-olds, t(14) = 3.4, pFDR<0.01).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to Figure 5B

claim: Spatiotemporal patterns of responses to different categories become reliable across infants after 6 months of age.
source: This suggests that spatiotemporal patterns of responses to different categories become reliable across infants after 6 months of age.
evidence: Interpretation of decoding results

claim: The LOOCV classifier successfully determined from spatiotemporal responses when infants were viewing faces in 64% of 4- to 6-month-olds, in 93% of 6- to 8-month-olds, and 87% of 12- to 15-month-olds.
source: Second, examination of classification by category shows that the LOOCV classifier successfully determined from spatiotemporal responses when infants were viewing faces in 64% of 4- to 6-month-olds, in 93% of 6- to 8-month-olds, and 87% of 12- to 15-month-olds (Figure 5C).
evidence: Analysis of classification performance with reference to Figure 5C

claim: Classification performance was numerically lower for categories other than faces (successful classification in less than 40% of the infants).
source: In contrast, classification performance was numerically lower for the other categories (successful classification in less than 40% of the infants).
evidence: Analysis of classification performance

claim: A reliable spatiotemporal response to faces that is consistent across infants develops after 4 months of age and dominates classification performance.
source: This suggests that a reliable spatiotemporal response to faces that is consistent across infants develops after 4 months of age and dominates classification performance.
evidence: Interpretation of classification results

claim: There is no reliable category information in individuals at 3- to 4-month-olds or 4- to 6-month-olds, as within-category similarity is not significantly above zero.
source: Examination of mean RSMs in each age group reveals no reliable category information in individuals at 3- to 4-month-olds or 4- to 6-month-olds, as within-category similarity is not significantly above zero (Figure 6A and 3- to 4-month-olds: on-diagonal, –0.03 ±0.06, p=0.96, one-tailed; 4- to 6-month-olds: on-diagonal: 0.009 ± 0.11, p=0.38).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to Figure 6A

claim: Within category similarity for faces is significantly above zero in 6- to 8-month-olds.
source: In particular, distributed responses to faces become reliable as within category similarity for faces is significantly above zero in 6- to 8-month-olds (Figure 6A, 0.31 ± 0.24, t(14) = 5.1, pFDR<0.05, FDR corrected over five category levels)
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to Figure 6A

claim: Within category similarity for faces stays reliable in 12- to 15-month-olds.
source: and stays reliable in 12- to 15-month-olds (Figure 6A, 0.26 ± 0.24, t(14) = 4.18, pFDR<0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to Figure 6A

claim: Within category similarity for limbs is significantly above zero in 12- to 15-months-olds.
source: Distributed responses to limbs become reliable later on as within category similarity for limbs is significantly above zero in 12- to 15-months-olds (Figure 6A, 0.11 ± 0.21, t(14) = 1.98, p=0.03, but not surviving FDR correction at five levels).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to Figure 6A

claim: In infants younger than 4 months (120 days) category distinctiveness is largely close to zero or even negative.
source: In infants younger than 4 months (120 days) category distinctiveness is largely close to zero or even negative, suggesting no differences between spatiotemporal responses to one category vs. another.
evidence: Observation from distinctiveness analysis

claim: Category distinctiveness increases with age and becomes more positive from 84 to 445 days of age.
source: Category distinctiveness increases with age and becomes more positive from 84 to 445 days of age (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Observation from distinctiveness analysis with reference to Figures 6B and C

claim: After approximately 6 months of age (194 days) face distinctiveness is consistently positive in individual infants (13/15 infants aged 194–364 days and 12/15 infants aged 365–445 days).
